snip.t: Pathologically, chronic pancreatitis is characterised by necro-inflammation, fibrosis, and loss of glandular tissue (atrophy)
Chronic pancreatitis (CP): Persistent inflammation leading to irreversible structural damage, fibrosis and loss of exocrine/endocrine function, often with recurrent attacks.
Pancreatic exocrine insufficiency: Chronic pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis, pancreatic TB — Lack of lipases, amylase, proteases → fat maldigestion

qs.q: A patient with suspected chronic pancreatitis presents with persistent steatorrhoea and weight loss. Which test measures exocrine pancreatic function and yields low levels in pancreatic insufficiency?
qs.e: Fecal elastase is low in pancreatic insufficiency caused by conditions like chronic pancreatitis or cancer. Serum amylase rises acutely and is not a measure of chronic exocrine insufficiency.

qs.q: Which tumour marker is monitored in pancreatic cancer, although it can also be elevated in benign conditions such as chronic pancreatitis and cholestasis?
qs.e: CA 19-9 is a tumour marker for pancreatic cancer that lacks specificity and can be elevated in cholestasis or chronic pancreatitis. CEA serves as a secondary tumour marker.

qs.q: A patient with a known history of chronic alcohol abuse and recurrent severe epigastric pain is evaluated for exocrine pancreatic insufficiency. Which of the following is the second most common overall cause of acute and chronic pancreatitis after gallstones?
qs.e: Gallstones are the most common cause of pancreatitis, followed closely by ethanol abuse as the second most common cause. Trauma and thiazide diuretics are less frequent causes listed in the mnemonic.

qs.q: A patient with chronic pancreatitis presents with greasy stools and weight loss. Is this presentation primarily categorized as maldigestion or malabsorption?
o: Secretory diarrhea caused by active epithelial electrolyte secretion
Osmotic diarrhea caused by unabsorbed luminal carbohydrate molecules
Malabsorption caused by inadequate mucosal transport of nutrients
Maldigestion caused by inadequate breakdown of dietary triglycerides
qs.e: Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency like chronic pancreatitis causes maldigestion, which is the inadequate breakdown of large molecules such as triglycerides. Malabsorption refers specifically to inadequate mucosal transport.

qs.q: A 54-year-old man with chronic pancreatitis and severe steatorrhea develops petechiae, ecchymoses, and an increased prothrombin time. Which fat-soluble vitamin deficiency is the primary cause of these bleeding manifestations?
qs.e: Vitamin K is required for the activation of clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X, leading to an elevated INR when depleted. Vitamin E deficiency causes hemolytic anemia and posterior column dysfunction rather than coagulation defects.

qs.q: A patient with chronic pancreatitis presents with chronic pain, steatorrhoea, weight loss, and newly diagnosed diabetes mellitus. What is the underlying pathophysiological mechanism for the development of steatorrhoea in this patient?
qs.e: Maldigestion and associated steatorrhoea in chronic pancreatitis result directly from insufficiency of the exocrine pancreas. Diabetes mellitus arises separately from endocrine pancreatic insufficiency.

qs.q: Which of the following is explicitly classified under uncommon aetiologies for chronic pancreatitis?
qs.e: Hypertriglyceridaemia is listed among the uncommon aetiologies of chronic pancreatitis, whereas alcohol consumption is classified as common. Smoking is noted as a lifestyle factor rather than a direct primary aetiology in that specific list.

qs.q: Which of the following long-term complications must clinicians actively monitor for in patients diagnosed with chronic pancreatitis?
qs.e: Patients with chronic pancreatitis require long-term monitoring for the development of pancreatic cancer. The other listed conditions are not direct complications of chronic pancreatic inflammation.

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Chronic pancreatitis is a progressive inflammatory disease of the pancreas that leads to irreversible fibrosis, exocrine and endocrine insufficiency. It is most often caused by alcohol abuse but also by genetic, metabolic, infectious and iatrogenic factors.

sections.p: Chronic pancreatitis is defined by persistent abdominal pain, pancreatic fibrosis on imaging, and evidence of exocrine or endocrine dysfunction. Diagnosis requires at least two of the following: characteristic pain, imaging evidence of fibrosis or ductal changes, and pancreatic function tests showing insufficiency.
b: Pain >3 months, epigastric, radiating to back

t.b: Measures exocrine function; <200 µg/g indicates insufficiency
Normal or mildly elevated; persistently high suggests acute flare
Detects calcifications, ductal strictures, mass effect; confirms fibrosis
Sensitive for early parenchymal changes and cysts

sections.p: Severity is staged by the M-ANNHEIM system, which grades pain, exocrine/endocrine insufficiency, imaging findings, and complications. Stages I–IV guide management intensity.
b: Stage I: mild pain, no insufficiency
Stage II: moderate pain, early insufficiency
Stage III: severe pain, significant insufficiency
Stage IV: complications like pseudocyst, ductal obstruction

sections.p: Alcohol abuse is the leading cause worldwide. Other important causes include hereditary mutations (PRSS1, SPINK1, CFTR), autoimmune pancreatitis, metabolic disorders, and infections common in low‑resource settings.
b: Pancreatic duct obstruction by stones or tumors

sections.p: Patients report dull, persistent epigastric pain that may worsen after meals. Weight loss, steatorrhoea, and diabetes are common. Pain may be episodic and can be triggered by alcohol or fatty foods.
Investigations aim to confirm fibrosis, assess function, and rule out mimics. In low‑resource settings, basic labs and ultrasound are useful when advanced imaging is unavailable.

t.b: Detects exocrine insufficiency; <200 µg/g indicates deficiency
Normal or mildly elevated; persistently high suggests acute flare
Shows ductal dilatation, stones; limited in detecting fibrosis
Best for fibrosis, calcifications, ductal strictures
Elevated in autoimmune pancreatitis; supports diagnosis

sections.p: Complications can be life‑threatening. Red flags include sudden severe pain, jaundice, vomiting, or unexplained weight loss. Complications include pseudocysts, ductal obstruction, diabetes, and pancreatic cancer.
b: Pancreatic cancer – consider in older patients with mass

sections.p: Management focuses on treating the underlying cause, controlling pain, replacing enzymes, and monitoring for complications. Alcohol cessation is paramount. Pain is managed with NSAIDs, opiates, or nerve blocks. Enzyme replacement improves nutrition.
b: Monitor for drug interactions with enzyme therapy

sections.p: Patients require regular follow‑up to assess pain, nutrition, glycaemic control, and imaging. Prevention focuses on alcohol avoidance, early detection of enzyme deficiency, and vaccination against hepatitis.
Chronic pancreatitis can mimic gallstone pancreatitis, peptic ulcer disease, and pancreatic cancer. Distinguishing features include chronic pain pattern, imaging findings, and enzyme levels.
b: Pancreatic cancer – weight loss, mass on imaging

sections.p: Low fecal elastase can be falsely normal in early disease; serum amylase/lipase may remain normal despite fibrosis. Imaging may miss early ductal changes; ultrasound is operator dependent.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe abdominal pain, jaundice, vomiting, unexplained weight loss, new‑onset diabetes, or signs of infection

faq.a: There is no cure; treatment focuses on stopping alcohol, managing pain, replacing enzymes, and monitoring complications.

faq.q: Why do patients develop diabetes in chronic pancreatitis?
faq.a: Fibrosis destroys insulin‑producing islet cells, leading to insulin deficiency.

faq.q: What is the role of enzyme replacement?
faq.a: It restores digestion of fats and proteins, reducing steatorrhoea and improving weight gain.
